What is IoC and DI?

IoC (Inversion of Control) is the principle: the framework controls object creation and lifecycle instead of your code. DI (Dependency Injection) is how Spring implements it: dependencies are given to an object rather than created by it. This gives loose coupling, easy testing with mocks, and swappable implementations.
Types of DI — which is recommended and why?

- Constructor (recommended): dependencies can be final and immutable, they're guaranteed present, the class is easy to unit test without Spring, and circular dependencies show up early. With a single constructor, @Autowired isn't needed.
- Setter: for optional dependencies.
- Field (@Autowired on a field): hides dependencies, can't be final, and is hard to test. Avoid it.
BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?

BeanFactory is the basic container. Beans are created lazily. ApplicationContext extends it and adds eager singleton creation, event publishing, i18n (MessageSource), AOP integration, environment and profiles, and automatic BeanPostProcessor registration. Always use ApplicationContext.
What are the bean scopes?

Scope | Description
singleton (default) | One instance per container
prototype | A new instance each time the bean is requested. Spring doesn't call its destroy callbacks
request | One per HTTP request
session | One per HTTP session
application | One per ServletContext
websocket | One per WebSocket session
💡 If you inject a prototype into a singleton, you only get one prototype instance. Use ObjectProvider<T>, @Lookup or a scoped proxy instead.
@Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller?

All of them are picked up by component scanning. @Service and @Controller are stereotypes (semantics only). @Repository also enables exception translation (SQLException → DataAccessException). @Controller is handled by Spring MVC, and @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody.
@Autowired, @Qualifier, @Primary — how does Spring resolve beans?

Spring injects by type. If several beans match, @Primary marks the default, @Qualifier("name") picks a specific one, and as a fallback the parameter name is matched against the bean name. If nothing matches you get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. If several match and none is chosen, you get NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Inject List<PaymentGateway> to receive all of them.
@Bean vs @Component?

@Component goes on your class and is found by scanning. @Bean goes on a method in a @Configuration class. Use it for third-party classes you can't annotate (RestTemplate, ObjectMapper) or for complex construction logic.
What is a circular dependency? How to fix it?

A → B → A. With constructor injection it fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. Since Spring Boot 2.6, circular references are prohibited by default. Fixes: redesign (extract a third class; this is the best option), use setter injection (needs spring.main.allow-circular-references=true on Boot 2.6+), use @Lazy on one dependency, or use events.
Explain @Transactional — propagation & isolation.

Propagation (what happens when a transactional method calls another):
- REQUIRED (default): join the existing transaction or start a new one.
- REQUIRES_NEW: suspend the current transaction and always start a new one (e.g. audit logs that must be saved even if the outer transaction rolls back).
- SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED, MANDATORY, NEVER, NESTED (savepoint).
Isolation: READ_UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads) → READ_COMMITTED → REPEATABLE_READ → SERIALIZABLE. The higher the level, the fewer anomalies (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) and the lower the concurrency.
Pitfalls: rollback happens only for unchecked exceptions by default (use rollbackFor for others). It works on non-private methods with class-based proxies since Spring 6.0 (public-only before that, and for interface proxies) called through the proxy, so self-invocation skips it. A try/catch that swallows the exception prevents the rollback. Use readOnly=true for queries.
What is AOP? Give real uses.

Aspect-Oriented Programming separates cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, security, caching, metrics, retries) from business code. Spring implements it with runtime proxies: JDK dynamic proxies for interfaces, CGLIB subclasses otherwise (the Boot default). @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async and @PreAuthorize are all built on AOP.
@Controller vs @RestController; @RequestParam vs @PathVariable vs @RequestBody?
How do you handle exceptions globally?
How does Spring Security work? Explain JWT flow.

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters (SecurityFilterChain). The flow is Authentication → AuthenticationManager → AuthenticationProvider → UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder, and the result is stored in the SecurityContextHolder (a ThreadLocal). Authorization uses authorizeHttpRequests rules or @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')").
What is the difference between @RequestMapping and @GetMapping?
@GetMapping is shorthand for @RequestMapping(method = GET). There are also Post, Put, Delete and Patch variants. @RequestMapping on a class sets the base path.
What are Spring profiles?

Profiles let you have environment-specific beans and config. Annotate with @Profile("dev"), use application-dev.yml, and activate with spring.profiles.active=prod (an environment variable, JVM argument or property).
How do you do validation in Spring?

Bean Validation (spring-boot-starter-validation): put constraints like @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size, @Email, @Min, @Pattern on DTO fields, then add @Valid to @RequestBody. Use @Validated on a class for method or group validation. For custom rules, write a @Constraint annotation with a ConstraintValidator.
What happens between new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(...) and the first usable bean?

The context registers internal post-processors, then refresh() runs. ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses configuration and creates bean definitions. All BeanPostProcessors are created. Non-lazy singletons are instantiated, populated and initialized, with proxies applied at the end. Finally ContextRefreshedEvent is published. Definitions always exist before instances, which is why a BeanFactoryPostProcessor can still change them.
BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor?

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor edits definitions once, before beans exist: for example, resolving ${...} or parsing @Configuration. A BeanPostProcessor sees every instance around initialization and may replace it, as the AOP auto-proxy creator does. Both are detected automatically by ApplicationContext. Their @Bean methods should be static.
Why does a @Transactional method called in @PostConstruct run without a transaction?

@PostConstruct runs in postProcessBeforeInitialization, before the proxy is created in postProcessAfterInitialization. The call also uses this. So no interceptor is involved. Move the work to an ApplicationReadyEvent listener, or a SmartInitializingSingleton that calls another bean, or use TransactionTemplate.
Explain the three-level cache. Why not two levels?

singletonObjects holds finished beans, earlySingletonObjects holds early references already handed out, and singletonFactories holds lambdas that produce early references. Two levels would suffice if beans were never proxied. Because a bean in a cycle may need a proxy, the injected early reference must already be that proxy. The factory delays this decision until a cycle really needs it, so normal beans keep the usual "proxy at the end" flow. The second level ensures the factory result is created once and shared.
Output: A has a field @Autowired B and an @Async method; B has a field @Autowired A. What happens?

It depends on creation order. Tested with spring.main.allow-circular-references at plain Spring's default: registering A first fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException: "has been injected into other beans in its raw version". Registering B first succeeds. When A is created first, B receives raw A as the early reference, then the async post-processor wraps A, so B would hold the wrong object. Spring detects this and aborts. When B is first, A is fully proxied before B needs it.
Why can't constructor injection use the early-reference trick? What can it do instead?

The early reference is the object produced by the constructor. In a constructor cycle, neither constructor can finish, so no object exists to expose. Instead, mark one parameter @Lazy, which injects a CGLIB proxy that finds the real bean on first use, or inject ObjectProvider<T>. Tested: with LA(@Lazy LB b) and LB(LA a), the context starts, and b is a CGLIB class. The best fix is still removing the cycle.
Output: singleton Sing has @Autowired Proto p, ObjectProvider<Proto> op, and a @Lookup method. Are repeated accesses the same instance?

Tested: s.direct() == s.direct() is true, since the field was injected once. op.getObject() == op.getObject() is false. s.look() == s.look() is false, because @Lookup is overridden to call getBean each time.
Are Spring singletons the same as the GoF Singleton? Are they thread-safe?

No to both. GoF means one instance per class loader. Spring means one instance per bean definition per container: two @Bean methods can create two singletons of one class, and two contexts hold separate ones. Spring adds no synchronization, so mutable fields are shared by all threads. Safe creation at startup is guaranteed, but not safe use.
Output: a @Configuration class has @Bean Repo repo() and two @Bean Svc methods that call repo(). How many Repo objects? And with proxyBeanMethods=false?

Tested. Full mode: one ("Repo created" prints once), a.r == b.r is true, because the CGLIB subclass intercepts repo(). Lite mode: three, one for the bean and two from plain Java calls, and a.r == b.r is false. The two extra objects are unmanaged: no injection, no proxies, no destroy callback.
What is the difference between @Primary, @Fallback, and @Qualifier?

@Primary is declared on a bean: "pick me when several match". @Fallback (Framework 6.2) is the opposite: "pick me only if nothing else does", which suits library defaults. @Qualifier is on the injection point and narrows the candidates first, so it overrides @Primary.
@Autowired vs @Resource vs @Inject?

@Autowired is Spring's: by type, then qualifiers, supports required=false. @Inject (Jakarta) behaves the same, without required. @Resource (Jakarta) goes by name first, falling back to type, and works on fields and setters. It is handy when you have several beans of a type and want one by name.
What is the difference between ${...} and #{...}?

${app.x} is resolved from the Environment by the placeholder mechanism. #{...} is evaluated by the SpEL engine and can call beans, do arithmetic and access static methods. They combine: #{'${app.hosts}'.split(',')}: placeholders are resolved first, then SpEL runs.
How do you run code after startup? Compare the options.

Option | When | Note
@PostConstruct | One bean is initialized | No proxy; other beans may not be ready
SmartInitializingSingleton | All singletons exist | Fine for internal wiring
ContextRefreshedEvent | Context refreshed | May fire multiple times, including from child contexts
CommandLineRunner (Boot) | After start, before ready | Failure stops the app
ApplicationReadyEvent (Boot) | App is accepting traffic | For background tasks
Are application events synchronous? What happens if a listener throws?

Synchronous by default: publishEvent returns only when all listeners finish. The listener shares the caller's thread and transaction, so an exception propagates to the publisher, stops later listeners, and may roll back the transaction. Use @Async to detach, or @TransactionalEventListener to run after the commit. You can also set an executor on the multicaster, but that makes every listener async, including ones that assumed otherwise.
You publish an event in a method with no @Transactional and a @TransactionalEventListener does not fire. Why?

The listener registers a synchronization with the current transaction. No transaction means nothing to synchronize with, so the event is dropped and only a debug message is logged. Tested: the event from the non-transactional method never arrived. Set fallbackExecution = true, or fix the transaction boundary.
Output: one aspect with @Around, @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing; the method succeeds. What is the order?

Tested on 6.2: around-before, before, method, afterReturning, after, around-after. On an exception: around-before, before, method, afterThrowing, after, around-catch. Since 5.2.7, @After runs after @AfterReturning and @AfterThrowing in the same aspect. Do not write tests that depend on two same-type advices in one aspect, whose order is undefined.
Which proxy does Spring use, and why does Boot default to CGLIB?

Plain Spring uses a JDK proxy when the bean implements an interface, and CGLIB otherwise. Boot sets spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true, so always CGLIB. The reason is usability: with JDK proxies, injecting the concrete class fails, and a bean's type would change when someone adds @Transactional. CGLIB's limits are final classes and methods.
Output: a bean with a final method is proxied. What does the final method return?

Tested with a field String nf = "field": nonfin() returns field; fin() returns null with no advice run; reading bean.nf directly returns null. The final method cannot be overridden, so it runs on the proxy object, which was created by Objenesis without running constructors or initializers. Any injected field would be null too, giving an NPE.
Can Spring AOP advise private methods, static methods, or objects you created with new?

No. Proxies only exist for container-managed beans, and a subclass can only override non-private, non-static, non-final methods. For these cases use AspectJ weaving. @Configurable with AspectJ can inject into objects built by new.
How would you build a @RateLimited or @Timed annotation?
Walk through what @Transactional does at runtime, step by step.

The caller hits the proxy. TransactionInterceptor reads attributes. getTransaction applies propagation: for a new transaction it takes a connection, sets auto-commit off, sets isolation and read-only, and binds the connection to the thread. The target method runs; JdbcTemplate or the EntityManager uses the thread-bound resource. For JPA, commit triggers a flush. On an exception, rollback rules are evaluated. Finally the resource is unbound and the connection is released.
Output: outer @Transactional inserts, calls inner @Transactional (REQUIRED) that throws, and outer catches. What happens?

Tested. Outer prints "caught" and returns, then its commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only. No rows remain. The inner interceptor marked the shared transaction rollback-only. To tolerate the failure, use REQUIRES_NEW or NESTED on the inner method, or do not use a transaction there.
Output: outer inserts 'outer', calls inner REQUIRES_NEW which inserts 'new' and commits, then outer throws. What is left?

Only new (tested). The inner transaction committed on its own connection before the outer failed. In the opposite case, inner REQUIRES_NEW throws and outer catches: only outer remains, and no UnexpectedRollbackException, because the transactions are independent. NESTED gives that same result here, through a savepoint, but an outer rollback would also undo the nested work.
A method throws IOException from a @Transactional method. Does it roll back?

No. It is checked, so the transaction commits and the exception still reaches the caller. Tested: the row was present after the exception. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class, or wrap the exception in a runtime exception.
Is @Transactional still limited to public methods?

This older rule is outdated. Since Framework 6.0, protected and package-visible methods are transactional with class-based proxies; a test confirmed this for a package-private method on 6.2. JDK proxies still need interface methods, which are public, and private and final methods never work. Reactive transaction methods, and those in interface-based proxies, must still be public.
Should @Transactional go on the controller, service, or repository?

On the service: it defines the business unit of work, which may span several repositories. On a controller, it keeps a connection during serialization and external calls. On repositories alone, each call commits separately. Spring Data repositories have their own for single calls. Keep the transaction as short as possible, with no remote calls inside.
How do you write to a database and send a Kafka message atomically?

There is no shared transaction, and @Transactional covers only the database. Sending before the commit may publish something that gets rolled back; sending after the commit may lose the message on a crash. The standard answer is the transactional outbox: insert the message into an outbox table in the same transaction, and a relay or CDC tool such as Debezium publishes it. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.
How do you handle two data sources with transactions?

Define two DataSource beans, two EntityManagerFactory or JDBC setups, and two transaction managers, one @Primary. Select with @Transactional("reportingTm"). A method using one manager does not cover the other. A two-phase commit needs JTA and is usually avoided; use a saga or outbox. For read/write routing, use AbstractRoutingDataSource wrapped in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so that the read-only flag is known before a connection is chosen.
Production shows "Connection is not available, request timed out" under load. How do you diagnose it?

Connections are held too long or leaked. Check hikaricp.connections.active and pending; set leakDetectionThreshold; take a thread dump to see what holders do. Usual causes: remote calls inside a transaction, Open Session in View keeping the connection through rendering, REQUIRES_NEW pool deadlock, or slow queries. Fix the cause before increasing the pool.
Describe the request path through DispatcherServlet, including argument resolution.

Filters run, then doDispatch. The HandlerMapping returns handler plus interceptors. preHandle runs. RequestMappingHandlerAdapter asks resolvers for each argument, using message converters for bodies, and runs validation. The method runs. Return handlers write the body with a converter chosen by Accept, or a view is rendered. postHandle and afterCompletion follow. Any exception goes to the HandlerExceptionResolver chain.
How does Spring choose the HttpMessageConverter?

For reading: the first converter whose canRead accepts the parameter type and Content-Type. None gives 415. For writing: it intersects the Accept header with what the converters can produce for the return type and the mapping's produces, picks the most specific media type, then the first converter that can write it. None gives 406. Extending configureMessageConverters replaces the defaults; in Boot, declare an HttpMessageConverter bean to add one.
Filter vs Interceptor: which would you use for authentication, request logging, and tenant resolution?

Authentication: a filter, as Spring Security does, since it must also protect static resources and unmapped paths. Request body logging: a filter, because it can wrap the request. Tenant resolution that needs the handler's annotations: an interceptor. If a business rule needs arguments: an aspect.
Why doesn't @RestControllerAdvice catch exceptions from my servlet filter or for authentication failures?

It runs inside DispatcherServlet, and filters run outside it. Handle errors in the filter itself; in Spring Security use AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler. A filter can also delegate to a HandlerExceptionResolver bean named handlerExceptionResolver to reuse the same handlers.
@Valid vs @Validated? Why is my @Min on a @RequestParam ignored, or not?

@Valid is the standard and cascades to nested objects. @Validated is Spring's, adding groups and, on a class, method-level validation via a proxy. Before Framework 6.1, a constraint directly on a controller parameter needed @Validated on the class, and failed with ConstraintViolationException. Since 6.1, Spring does it natively and raises HandlerMethodValidationException. A missed @Valid on a nested field is the classic cause of "nested validation is ignored".
How would you upload a 2 GB file without running out of memory?

Do not buffer it. MultipartFile.getBytes() loads it all into the heap. Options: use the input stream and copy to storage; raise limits; or best, give the client a presigned object-storage URL so the file bypasses the app. Support resumable or chunked upload for flaky networks. Validate size and type, scan content, and generate the stored name yourself.
RestClient vs WebClient: which would you choose in a servlet app?

RestClient for ordinary calls: blocking, simple, shares the same message converters. WebClient pulls in WebFlux and reactive types, and earns that when you need concurrent fan-out or streaming. With virtual threads, you can even get concurrency with RestClient in simple tasks. Both need timeouts, and a shared configured builder.
What is backpressure, and what happens without it?

Backpressure lets a consumer signal how much it can accept, using request(n). Without it, a fast producer forces the consumer to buffer without bound, or drop data, until memory runs out. Reactor offers onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureDrop and limitRate. It works across the network only when the protocol supports it, for example via TCP flow control.
Output: what does this print? Mono.just("x").map(v -> (String) null).onErrorResume(e -> { print(e.getClass()); return Mono.just("y"); }).subscribe(print)

Tested: NullPointerException, then y. Reactive Streams forbids null elements, so a mapper returning null becomes an error signal. For "no value", use mapNotNull or return Mono.empty() from a flatMap. Similarly, Mono.empty().map(...) never runs the mapper, and .defaultIfEmpty("empty!") supplies the value.
subscribeOn vs publishOn?

subscribeOn sets the thread on which the subscription and source run, wherever it appears in the chain. The first one nearest the source wins. publishOn switches the thread for operators after it, and can appear several times. Use subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) to wrap blocking sources.
When would you not choose WebFlux?

When the app uses JDBC/JPA, has ordinary CRUD load, or the team has little reactive experience. Debugging and stack traces are harder, one blocking call does serious harm, and every dependency must be non-blocking. Virtual threads now meet most high-concurrency needs in the blocking model. It remains a good fit for gateways and streaming.
@Cacheable returned stale data after an update. What are the likely causes?

- The update method lacks @CachePut or @CacheEvict, or uses a different key.
- The evict is self-invoked, so it never ran.
- Local cache on several instances: only one was evicted. Use Redis, or pub/sub invalidation.
- The eviction ran before commit and a reader re-cached old data.
- A @Query or another service wrote directly to the database.
Output: what does @Cacheable do with a null return? How do you avoid caching nulls?

By default, most providers store a null marker, and subsequent calls return null without running the method. This protects against penetration by repeated lookups of absent ids, but can hide newly added rows. Use unless = "#result == null". An Optional return is unwrapped automatically for this check.
fixedRate vs fixedDelay vs cron, and what if a job takes longer than its interval?

fixedRate measures start to start. fixedDelay measures end to next start. cron uses calendar times. An overrunning job does not overlap itself; the next run starts late. With the default single scheduler thread, other jobs wait as well. If @Async is added, runs can overlap.
Your app runs 5 replicas and a nightly @Scheduled job sends emails. What goes wrong and how do you fix it?

All five run it, so customers get five emails. Options: ShedLock with @SchedulerLock and a database or Redis lock, Quartz with a clustered job store, a dedicated Kubernetes CronJob, or a leader election. Make the job idempotent regardless, for example by marking rows as sent, since locks can expire during long runs.
Why might an @Async pool with core 5, max 50 and default queue never exceed 5 threads?

ThreadPoolExecutor adds non-core threads only when the queue rejects a task. ThreadPoolTaskExecutor's default queue capacity is Integer.MAX_VALUE, so it never fills. Tasks pile up, latency grows, and memory may run out. Set a bounded queue and a rejection policy such as CallerRunsPolicy for natural backpressure.
Why is SecurityContextHolder empty in my @Async method?

The context is in a ThreadLocal, and the task runs on another thread. Wrap the executor in DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor, or set a TaskDecorator. Spring's ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator with Micrometer context propagation handles observability data. The same applies to MDC and request attributes.
How does a Spring Data interface with no implementation work?

@EnableJpaRepositories (automatic in Boot) scans for repository interfaces and registers a JpaRepositoryFactoryBean for each, which builds a proxy. Inherited CRUD methods are delegated to SimpleJpaRepository. For query methods, QueryLookupStrategy at startup parses the name into a PartTree, or reads @Query, and prepares a query. A typo in a property name fails at startup.
What are the main changes in Spring Framework 6 and 7?

6.x: Java 17 baseline, Jakarta EE 9+ (jakarta.*), AOT and native image support, ProblemDetail, @HttpExchange, RestClient (6.1), virtual thread support (6.1), @Fallback and @MockitoBean (6.2). 7.0: still Java 17 minimum, Jakarta EE 11, null-safety through JSpecify annotations, first-class API versioning in MVC and WebFlux, BeanRegistrar, core retry and concurrency-limit resilience annotations, and @ImportHttpServices.
Design: an order must update stock, charge a card, and send email. How do you structure transactions in Spring?

Keep the database transaction small: validate, create the order in PENDING state, and reserve stock in one @Transactional method. Charge outside the transaction with an idempotency key and timeouts. Update the status in a second short transaction. Send the email from an AFTER_COMMIT listener or, for guarantees, via an outbox. On failure, a compensating action releases the stock. This avoids holding locks and connections during slow external calls.
FactoryBean vs BeanFactory?

BeanFactory is the container: the root interface that holds and creates beans. FactoryBean is one bean inside the container that produces another object. Asking for "client" gives you getObject()'s result, and "&client" gives you the factory. 💡 Mention a real example: each Spring Data repository is produced by a RepositoryFactoryBean.
How should @Retryable and @Transactional be combined?

The retry must sit outside the transaction. Each attempt then runs in a fresh transaction, after the failed one has rolled back. If the retry is inside, it retries against a transaction that is already marked rollback-only or holds a broken connection. The simplest way is to put @Retryable on a caller bean that calls the @Transactional service. You can also order the advisors so that retry has higher precedence. Retry only transient errors, such as deadlock, lock timeout or optimistic lock failure. Never retry validation errors.
Which operations are safe to retry automatically?

Only idempotent ones: GET, PUT, DELETE, or POST with an idempotency key. Retrying a non-idempotent "charge card" call after a timeout can charge the customer twice, because the first request may have succeeded. Also cap the attempts, use exponential backoff with jitter so that clients do not all retry together, and respect Retry-After. Never retry 4xx errors except 408, 425 and 429. Retries in several layers multiply: 3 retries in each of 3 layers make 27 calls.
ResponseEntity vs @ResponseStatus vs ResponseStatusException?

- ResponseEntity<T>: full control of status, headers and body per call, for example ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto).
- @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) on a handler: a fixed status. On an exception class, it maps that exception to a status.
- throw new ResponseStatusException(NOT_FOUND, "Order 7"): an ad-hoc error status without a custom exception class. It renders as ProblemDetail.
In larger codebases, prefer domain exceptions with one @RestControllerAdvice, so that the status mapping lives in one place.
How do you accept a password in a request but never return it?

The best approach is separate request and response DTOs: CreateUserRequest has the password, and UserResponse does not. If you must share one class, use @JsonProperty(access = JsonProperty.Access.WRITE_ONLY). @JsonIgnore would block it in both directions. Never serialize JPA entities directly. You risk leaking fields and lazy-loading errors, and every schema change becomes an API change.
Why are my LocalDateTime values serialized as arrays like [2025,1,31,10,0]?

Jackson's WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS feature is on, or the Java time module is missing, because the ObjectMapper was created with new ObjectMapper() rather than Spring Boot's auto-configured one. Boot registers the Java time module and turns off timestamps, so dates are written as ISO-8601 strings. Inject the Boot mapper, or customize it, instead of creating your own. For APIs, prefer Instant or OffsetDateTime, which keep the offset, over LocalDateTime, which does not.
Spring AOP vs AspectJ weaving?

| Spring AOP | AspectJ
How | Runtime proxy around a bean | Bytecode weaving at compile, post-compile or load time
Join points | Method execution on Spring beans only | Methods, constructors, field access, static initialisers
Self-invocation (this.foo()) | Not advised, bypasses the proxy | Advised
Private, final, objects made with new | Not advised | Advised
Setup | Starter dependency only | Compiler plugin or a -javaagent
Rule of thumb: Spring AOP covers transactions, caching, security and logging on service methods. Pick AspectJ only when you must advise what proxies cannot reach. Both use the same @Aspect annotation style.
@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties vs Environment?
@EventListener vs @TransactionalEventListener?

| @EventListener | @TransactionalEventListener
Runs | Immediately, inside publishEvent() | At a transaction phase, AFTER_COMMIT by default
No transaction active | Runs normally | Skipped, unless fallbackExecution = true
Exception in listener | Propagates to the publisher and can roll back its transaction | After commit it cannot undo the commit
Writing to the DB | Joins the publisher's transaction | After commit, needs REQUIRES_NEW to persist anything
Typical use | In-process side effects that must be atomic with the work | Emails, cache eviction, messages after data is safe
Rule of thumb: if the side effect must only happen when the data is really saved, use @TransactionalEventListener. If losing it on a crash is unacceptable, use an outbox table instead.
@Cacheable vs @CachePut vs @CacheEvict?
